docs.title: Relation-Oriented Programming
docs.text:
Six essays on why halfORM is built the way it is.

I started building halfORM, a Python library for PostgreSQL, in 2015. Since 2018 we've been using it in production at work, on several projects.

The reference documentation says what halfORM does. These pages say why the design takes the shape it does, and what it refuses to do. They are an argument, not a tutorial: each one takes a known failure mode of object-relational mapping and shows what happens to it when the schema, rather than the application, holds authority over the structure of the data access layer.

The thesis, in one sentence: the structural problems of ORM follow from a design direction rather than from implementation quality, and inverting the direction makes them impossible rather than merely manageable.

Each essay stands on its own. Read them in order for the argument, or pick the one that names a problem you have.

docs.title: The series
docs.text: Essay What it covers 1 The Vietnam of Computer Science, Twenty Years On Ted Neward's 2006 diagnosis, the seven failure modes it catalogues, and why twenty years of engineering has not dissolved them. 2 A Relation Is a Predicate, Not an Object The core abstraction. Set algebra on Python objects, deferred execution, and what happens to __eq__ when equality means set equality. 3 You Can't Have an N+1 Problem if Navigation Isn't a Query Foreign-key navigation as join construction, with no configuration and no fetch strategy to tune. 4 Delete Your Repository Layer Predicate locality: why query logic can live on the relation class once there is no session, and what that does to code organisation. 5 halfORM vs SQLAlchemy Core vs Django ORM Three queries side by side, including the one where halfORM loses. 6 Git Is the Migration Tool Schema and code in one commit, patches in plain SQL, and a repository checkout that carries the database itself, not instructions for rebuilding it.

docs.title: The running example
docs.text:
Every essay from part 2 onwards draws on the same four tables. A series arguing that the schema is the source of truth should start by showing the schema:

CREATE TABLE blog.author (
    id    UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    name  TEXT NOT NULL,
    email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE blog.post (
    id        UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    title     TEXT NOT NULL,
    content   TEXT,
    published BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    author_id UUID REFERENCES blog.author(id)
);

CREATE TABLE blog.comment_type (
    name TEXT PRIMARY KEY
);

CREATE TABLE blog.comment (
    id           UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    content      TEXT NOT NULL,
    post_id      UUID REFERENCES blog.post(id),
    author_id    UUID REFERENCES blog.author(id),
    comment_type TEXT REFERENCES blog.comment_type(name)
);

Four foreign keys, three of them converging on comment, one lookup table, no Python. That is the whole model declaration: halfORM introspects it at startup and the classes named in the essays (Author, Post, Comment, CommentType) are what comes back.

A larger and fully runnable variant, with a second schema for identity, is in Simple Blog.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
These essays argue a position and name its costs. Every one of them states what the design gives up: no cache, PostgreSQL only, no scalar aggregation without a view, a migration workflow whose guarantee is procedural rather than structural.

They are not release notes and do not track the API. Where an essay touches something the reference documentation specifies, it links there; Fundamentals is the authority on the model, and Learn halfORM in half an hour is the place to start if you want to write code rather than read an argument.

docs.title: halfORM vs SQLAlchemy Core vs Django ORM
docs.text:
Part 5 of six in Relation-Oriented Programming. Series index

Let me declare the bias first: I wrote halfORM. Everything below is a structural comparison chosen to illustrate a design claim, not a neutral evaluation of three libraries. There's no benchmark here and no user study. I've included the case where halfORM comes off worst, because a comparison that only shows wins isn't worth reading.

The two reference points are the dominant styles of Python data access. SQLAlchemy Core is a SQL expression builder and the closest structural peer here, since both defer execution and compose expressions. Django ORM is the full code-first ORM. Peewee, PonyORM and Tortoise are all code-first with model class declarations and condition-level composition, so they'd sit next to Django in every row below.

All examples use a four-table blog schema: author, post, comment, comment_type, whose DDL is in the series index. In the SQLAlchemy listings, post / author / comment are Table objects declared with autoload_with=engine.

The underlying difference is what the composable unit is:

  • SQLAlchemy Core composes column expressions (post.c.published == True) and Select statements.
  • Django ORM composes Q objects and __ path expressions.
  • halfORM composes relation predicates: an object carrying its table, its constraints, and its join structure.

That distinction sounds academic until you try to reuse something.

docs.title: Query 1: set difference
docs.text:
Authors who have never posted.

halfORM:

Author() - Post().fk_author()

SQLAlchemy Core, with no set-difference operator on Select objects, needs a subquery:

select(author).where(
    ~author.c.id.in_(
        select(post.c.author_id).where(post.c.author_id.isnot(None))
    )
)

Django ORM has no set-difference operator either; exclude with a subquery:

Author.objects.exclude(id__in=Post.objects.values('author_id'))

All three work. The difference is that one of them is the relational operation you actually meant, written once, with a -.

docs.title: Query 2: predicate reuse
docs.text:
This is the one that matters.

In halfORM a Relation is a value. Name it, store it, pass it around, compose it into different things; no query runs until a terminal method does:

published   = Post(published=True)               # a value
alice_posts = Author(name='Alice').rfk_posts()   # a value

published & alice_posts                # published posts by Alice
published.rfk_comments().fk_author()   # commenters on published posts

published is reused in two structurally different queries. It carries its own join structure, so nothing has to be restated.

SQLAlchemy Core: published_cond is a column expression. It carries no join structure. Each reuse restates the joins:

published_cond = post.c.published == True

# Reuse 1: join restated
select(post).join(author, post.c.author_id == author.c.id) \
            .where(and_(published_cond, author.c.name == 'Alice'))

# Reuse 2: two joins restated
select(author).join(comment, comment.c.author_id == author.c.id) \
              .join(post, comment.c.post_id == post.c.id) \
              .where(published_cond)

Django Q objects are composable and their __ paths do resolve to joins, but the join structure comes from the QuerySet context, not from the Q object. A Q written for one starting relation can't cross over to another:

published = Q(published=True)
alice_q   = Q(author__name='Alice')

Post.objects.filter(published & alice_q)               # context 1: fine
Author.objects.filter(comment__post__published=True)   # context 2: `published`
                                                       # cannot be reused here

The halfORM version of that second query is published.rfk_comments().fk_author(): the same published object, in a different composition.

docs.title: Query 3: multi-hop navigation
docs.text:
Authors who commented on published posts.

halfORM, with no join conditions at all, because they're in the catalog:

Post(published=True).rfk_comments().fk_author()

SQLAlchemy Core, with every join condition explicit:

select(author) \
    .join(comment, comment.c.author_id == author.c.id) \
    .join(post, comment.c.post_id == post.c.id) \
    .where(post.c.published == True)

Django is concise, and the filter itself generates a single JOIN query:

authors = Author.objects.filter(comment__post__published=True)

Credit where due: that's a good line. The problem is downstream, when you traverse the results:

for author in authors:
    for comment in author.comment_set.all():   # N queries
        print(comment.post.title)              # N more queries

# Fix: explicit opt-in, restating the full traversal path
Author.objects.filter(comment__post__published=True) \
              .prefetch_related('comment_set__post')

Both Django ORM and SQLAlchemy's ORM layer return model instances rather than dictionaries, which brings back the identity, session, and lazy-loading questions from part 1 of this series.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
What the developer must state explicitly:

Set difference Predicate reuse Multi-hop Schema declaration Result type N+1 by default halfORM - operator compose once 0 join conditions none dicts not expressible SQLAlchemy Core subquery restate joins explicit joins Table per relation dicts no Django ORM filter/exclude restate path __ traversal model class model instances yes, unless prefetch

The "schema declaration" column is the one that compounds. SQLAlchemy Core with autoload_with populates column metadata from the live database automatically, but you still need one Table variable per relation and you still write join conditions by hand. automap_base() goes further and generates mapped classes from a live schema, but it targets the ORM layer, so what you get back carries the identity map, the session, and the lazy loading that this whole design is trying to avoid. halfORM's database-first stance isn't unique; the combination of introspection-only, relation-level predicates, and no session management doesn't have a direct equivalent in the Python ecosystem that I know of.

docs.title: Where halfORM loses: scalar aggregation
docs.text:
Two things travel under the name "aggregation", and halfORM handles exactly one of them.

Collecting related rows it does natively. ho_select(json_agg=...), from part 3, compiles to a LEFT JOIN plus json_agg plus a GROUP BY on the primary key, and returns each author with their posts nested inside the row. It follows FK chains, and takes a distinct flag for when an intermediate join multiplies rows. No view required.

Reducing them to one number per group it does not. Annotate every author with their post count. Django:

Author.objects.annotate(post_count=Count('post'))

One expression. Django infers the LEFT OUTER JOIN and the GROUP BY from the declared foreign key. It's exactly right, and it's the kind of thing you write constantly.

halfORM has no equivalent. There is no COUNT, SUM or AVG to project per group, no HAVING to filter on the result, and no window functions; correlated subqueries are outside what relation-oriented composition expresses too. (ho_count() counts the extension of one predicate, which is a different question.)

You can get close by counting the aggregated list in Python:

authors = Author()
authors.rfk_posts.set()
for row in authors.ho_select(json_agg={'rfk_posts': ['id']}):
    post_count = len(row['rfk_posts'])

That works, and it is the wrong tool for the job. It ships every post id across the wire to compute a number the database could have returned by itself, and the count exists only once the rows arrive, so it cannot narrow the query: there is no way to ask for authors with more than ten posts and have the database do the filtering. The recommended answer is a view:

CREATE VIEW blog.author_post_count AS
  SELECT a.*, count(p.id) AS post_count
  FROM author a
  LEFT JOIN post p ON p.author_id = a.id
  GROUP BY a.id;

and then use it like any other relation, because halfORM doesn't distinguish tables from views:

APC = blog.get_relation_class('blog.author_post_count')
APC(post_count=('>', 10)).ho_count()

Is that better or worse? Honestly: it depends on who you are.

The cost is real: you write and maintain a view, you need DDL rights or a DBA, and a one-liner became a two-step. If you're a solo developer on a greenfield project, Django's version is plainly more convenient.

The benefit is also real: the view is available to every client of that database, not just your Python app; it's version-controlled alongside the schema; it's readable by anyone who knows SQL; and the query planner sees it as SQL rather than as generated ORM output. If three services query this database and two of them aren't in Python, the view is the only version of this logic that all three can share.

So it's a position, not an oversight: complex query logic belongs in the database, expressed in the language designed for it. But you should know you're choosing it.

The same escape hatches exist for everything else: model.execute_function() and model.call_procedure() for stored routines, model.execute_query() for arbitrary parameterised SQL returning dicts.

docs.title: When not to use halfORM
docs.text:
Since this is the comparison post, the fit question belongs here.

Don't use it if you need to support more than one database engine. halfORM is PostgreSQL-only, deliberately and irreversibly: views, native table inheritance and advanced types are all what makes the rest work.

Don't use it if your project is code-first and you like it that way. If your team's model is "the Python classes are the schema", halfORM inverts your entire workflow and you will fight it every day.

Don't use it if you're in Django. Django's ORM is woven into forms, the admin, auth, and the migration system. Swapping it out means giving up the parts of Django people use Django for.

Do consider it if your team is comfortable with SQL, you treat PostgreSQL as a first-class component rather than a generic storage backend, and you work against schemas that exist independently of your application: because someone else owns them, because several applications share them, or because they predate your code.

That last case is the one halfORM was built for, and it's more common in enterprise settings than the greenfield-project literature suggests.

For a hands-on comparison of your own, Learn halfORM in half an hour.

docs.title: Git Is the Migration Tool
docs.text:
Part 6 of six in Relation-Oriented Programming. Series index

The examples use the four-table blog schema of the running example: author, post, comment, comment_type.

The first five essays in this series were about runtime: what a data access layer looks like when the live schema is the sole source of truth. This one is about time. Schemas change. Code that uses them has to change with them. That's the ownership problem, and it's on a different axis from everything else: it isn't dissolved by removing a concept, because there's no concept to remove. It has to be dissolved by a workflow that makes the bad situation unreachable.

Three things go wrong.

Ownership. In code-first ORMs the application claims authority over the schema: edit a class, generate a migration, the database follows. Fine until a second application shares the schema, or a DBA adds an index, or the schema predates your code by a decade. In database-first tools the database owns the schema but nothing propagates changes back into application code: rename a column and every query referencing it breaks, some loudly, some silently.

Drift. Any code generator that reads a schema will, on its next run, overwrite whatever you wrote into the generated files. So either you never regenerate, and your code drifts from the schema, or you regenerate and lose your work.

Atomicity. The migration that renames a column must deploy simultaneously with the code that uses the new name. Not "shortly after". Simultaneously. Most setups achieve this with deployment discipline and hope.

half-orm-dev drives all of this through half_orm dev, and is built on two choices that together make all three unreachable: SQL is the patch language, and git is the versioning infrastructure. Everything else follows.

docs.title: Choice 1: patches are SQL files
docs.text:
A patch is a directory of .sql and .py files, applied in lexicographic order. .sql files do the DDL and in-place data transformations, and are typically written by the DBA. .py files handle migrations that need to iterate over rows or touch the Python model, and are written by the developer. A patch with no schema change contains only .py files.

Not a Python function à la Alembic. Not a Java method à la Flyway. Not an XML descriptor à la Liquibase.

The argument is the same one as for queries. The relational model already has a complete, precise, standard language for describing schema changes. Layering a Python or Java DSL on top adds an abstraction that can be wrong (the generated SQL may not be what you meant), requires the migration framework to be installed and understood to read your own history, and severs the connection between the artefact you wrote and the statement that ran.

This trades away real things. Flyway, Liquibase and Alembic give you automatic rollback generation, cross-DBMS portability, and structured validation pipelines that plain SQL files don't provide. What you get in exchange is directness and auditability: a patch file can be read in any editor, applied with psql, and understood by anyone who knows SQL, which, for a schema change, is everyone who should be reviewing it.

There is exactly one thing patches are not for, and it gets its own directory. bootstrap/ at the project root holds .sql and .py files that run in alphabetic order, once, when a brand-new instance is created by half_orm dev clone, immediately after the schema is restored. They never run on patch apply, patch merge, release promote or upgrade: nothing resets the database between those, so a script that is not independently idempotent would corrupt it the second time through.

What belongs there is what is specific to this instance: the first admin account, a per-site secret. What does not is reference data every instance should carry. A new system role is a patch, written as idempotent DML like any other; it reaches existing instances through upgrade and is captured in the release's data snapshot, which bootstrap/ scripts never are.

The distinction matters more than it looks. Anything shared travels the patch path, which is versioned, reviewed and replayed identically everywhere. bootstrap/ is the deliberate exception for what cannot be shared, and keeping it that narrow is what stops it becoming a second, unaudited migration channel.

docs.title: Choice 2: the zone discipline
docs.text:
half_orm dev patch apply is the atomic unit of the whole workflow, and it does not work incrementally. It restores the database from the production baseline, replays every patch already staged for the release, applies the files of the patch you are working on in order, then introspects the updated live schema and regenerates the model classes. When it returns, the Python model reflects the schema exactly, and it does so from a known starting point rather than from whatever your local database had drifted into.

That rebuild is why the command can be run again and again while you write the patch. Getting a statement wrong costs you nothing: fix the file, run it again, and the database is rebuilt from the baseline with your correction in place.

That regeneration is exactly the destructive step described above. What makes it safe is that every generated file is split by sentinel comments into two regions:

  • The generated zone holds introspected columns, the primary key description, and the foreign-key graph. Overwritten unconditionally, every time.
  • The developer zone holds Fkeys aliases, @singleton guards, and business methods. Never touched. Ever.
from half_orm.model import register
from blog import MODEL, ho_baseclasses

#>>> PLACE YOUR CODE BELOW THIS LINE.       # developer zone (module level)
#<<< PLACE YOUR CODE ABOVE THIS LINE.

@register                                    # generated
class Post(ho_baseclasses.BC_BlogPost):
    """
    FIELDS:
    - id:        (uuid) NOT NULL
    - title:     (text) NOT NULL
    - content:   (text)
    - published: (bool) NOT NULL
    - author_id: (uuid)

    PRIMARY KEY (id)
    FOREIGN KEYS:
    - _reverse_fkey_blog_blog_comment_post_id: ("id")
    - post_author_id_fkey: ("author_id")
    """
    #>>> PLACE YOUR CODE BELOW THIS LINE.    # developer zone (class level)
    Fkeys = {
        'rfk_comments': '_reverse_fkey_blog_blog_comment_post_id',
        'fk_author':    'post_author_id_fkey',
    }
    #<<< PLACE YOUR CODE ABOVE THIS LINE.

    def __init__(self, id=None, title=None, content=None,   # generated
                 published=None, author_id=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(id=id, title=title, content=content,
                         published=published, author_id=author_id, **kwargs)
        #>>> PLACE YOUR CODE BELOW THIS LINE.
        # developer zone (__init__ + business code)

Drift becomes structurally impossible inside this workflow, because there is no state in which the generated zone is stale: it's rewritten on every patch, and rewriting it can't cost you anything, because your code isn't in it.

Note where the developer zone sits, by the way. It's where the business methods from part 4 go: the predicate-locality pattern isn't a convention you have to remember, it's where the tooling puts the cursor.

docs.title: What a change actually looks like
docs.text:
Add a NOT NULL constraint to blog.post.author_id:

$ half_orm dev patch create 7-post-author-id-should-be-not-null
$ cat > Patches/7-post-author-id-should-be-not-null/00_author_id_not_null.sql
alter table blog.post alter column author_id set not null;
$ half_orm dev patch apply
$ git diff
--- a/blog/blog/post.py
+++ b/blog/blog/post.py
@@ -36,7 +36,7 @@
     - title:     (text) NOT NULL
     - content:   (text)
     - published: (bool) NOT NULL
-    - author_id: (uuid)
+    - author_id: (uuid) NOT NULL

     PRIMARY KEY (id)

One line changed, in the generated zone. The Fkeys block two screens down is untouched. Then you write the business code and tests that use the new constraint, and commit. That single commit contains the SQL patch, the regenerated generated zones, and the new application code.

Schema version and code version cannot drift, because they are the same commit. That's the atomicity problem, gone, without a deployment checklist.

docs.title: Git as the authority, not a migrations table
docs.text:
Every half-orm-dev project is already a git repository. Python source, generated classes, business methods, and schema patches are all tracked together. So:

  • git diff v1.3.4..v1.4.0 shows the schema delta and the code delta in one reviewable diff.
  • git blame tells you when a column was introduced and by whom.
  • git bisect can find the patch that broke a schema-sensitive test.

None of that needs tooling beyond git.

The branch model:

ho-prod ─────●──────────────────────────────────●──────────►  (tags: v1.4.0)
              \                                /
   ho-release/1.4.0 ●──────────●──────────────●
                     \        /
        ho-patch/7-... ●────●
                             └─ merge moves Patches/7-.../ into Patches/staged/
                                and renames the branch to ho-staged/7-...

half_orm dev release create minor forks ho-release/X.Y.Z from ho-prod. half_orm dev patch create N-name forks a patch branch from the release. half_orm dev patch merge restores the production state, applies the accumulated patches, runs the full test suite (a failure aborts the merge), and on success merges into the release, renames the branch to ho-staged/N-name, and moves the patch directory from Patches/N-name/ to Patches/staged/N-name/. Repeat for as many patches as the release needs. half_orm dev release promote prod merges into ho-prod, tags vX.Y.Z, and deletes the staged and release branches.

That relocation is worth a word, because the reason is ergonomic rather than technical. A patch directory sits under Patches/ while it is a candidate, under Patches/staged/ once merged into a release, and under Patches/orphaned/ if it is detached from one. Without the move, Patches/ and the ho-patch/ namespace accumulate every patch the project has ever produced, and what a developer needs to see (what is still in flight) ends up buried in what is already settled. Status becomes readable from the layout instead: what sits directly under Patches/ is what remains to be merged.

The branch rename has a different motive. ho-staged/N-name holds nothing the release branch does not already have, and it is kept anyway: a merge that failed or completed only in part can still be examined afterwards, and a patch can still be backed out while its release is open. Once the release is promoted, nothing in it can move, and the staged branches go with it.

The tag is the schema version. The sequence of patch directories between two tags is the migration path.

This is where the difference from Flyway and Liquibase is sharpest. In those tools the migrations table in the database is the authoritative record of what has been applied; lose it and the tool can't compute what remains to run. In half-orm-dev that authority is git's. half_orm_meta.hop_release is a version stamp written after a successful upgrade, a derived record, not an input to the next computation.

Deploying a new instance is half_orm dev clone, which the next section covers. Upgrading an existing one is three steps with nothing to synchronise between them: pull, half_orm dev upgrade, restart. half_orm dev upgrade reads the current version from the metadata table and applies every patch between it and the target tag. It performs no regeneration at all: the Python model comes from the tag checkout, so schema version and code version are consistent by construction rather than by procedure.

Rollback is a branch switch, covered below with the branches it switches between.

docs.title: A checkout is a working instance
docs.text:
Everything so far says git holds the record. What makes that more than a filing claim is that the record is complete enough to instantiate.

Promoting a release to production writes a snapshot of the database into .hop/model/, committed and tagged with everything else:

.hop/model/
├── schema.sql          # relative symlink to the current version
├── schema-1.3.4.sql    # structure, from pg_dump --schema-only
├── data-1.3.4.sql      # the reference data the release's patches inserted
├── schema-1.4.0.sql
└── data-1.4.0.sql

Restore those two files into an empty database and you have that release, running. No patch replay, no migration order to respect, nothing to seed. A repository checkout is not a recipe for the database; it is the database, alongside the schema patches that produced it, the generated model, the business code and the tests.

That single artefact serves two audiences who are normally served separately, and it serves them with the same command. Production deploys a new instance with half_orm dev clone --production, which restores the snapshot and then runs the bootstrap/ scripts for what is specific to that instance. A developer joining the project runs the same command without the flag, gets the same structure and the same reference data locally, and every patch apply rebuilds from that snapshot before replaying the release's staged patches. The environment a developer tests against and the one operations deploys are produced from the same committed bytes, one flag apart.

It also explains the rule from earlier about where reference data belongs. A patch that inserts a system role as idempotent DML is captured in the next snapshot automatically, because the dump takes data as well as structure. It therefore reaches every future instance without anyone running anything, which is precisely what bootstrap/ scripts, running once per instance and never captured, cannot do.

Only production versions are snapshotted. Release candidates and staged states are not, hotfixes overwrite the version they fix, and git keeps the earlier snapshots for as long as the history does.

docs.title: What production checks out
docs.text:
The branch diagram above is the development side. A production server sees a different shape:

$ git branch
  ho-prod
  ho-prod-1.3.3
  ho-prod-1.3.4
* ho-prod-1.4.0

Promoting a release creates ho-prod-X.Y.Z from the tag and pushes it. The branch is immutable: nothing is ever committed to it afterwards. A server checks one out and runs it, which is why deployment needs no git write access anywhere on the machine, and why the starred branch is a sufficient statement of what that server is running.

Because each of those branches carries its own .hop/model/ snapshot, ho-prod-1.3.4 is not merely a label for a past release: check it out and the schema, the reference data, the generated model and the code of 1.3.4 are all there together. That is what makes rollback a branch switch. half_orm dev rollback restores the snapshot taken before the last upgrade and checks out the branch it belongs to, with --to-version to go further back. Nothing is rewritten and no inverse migration is computed: you return to a state that was released rather than to one reconstructed from deltas.

Three versions are kept. Promotion prunes the older ones from the remote, so the listing above is not an accumulation but the retention window itself.

This is also what a migrations table cannot give you. Reconstructing an old state there means replaying the project's deltas from its first commit onward and hoping each one still runs. Here it means checking out a tag.

docs.title: Tests run against a real schema, always
docs.text:
The workflow has a side effect. After half_orm dev patch apply, your local database is the patched schema, so tests written at that point exercise the new constraints against real PostgreSQL behaviour. At merge time the suite runs against the schema production actually runs.

Because halfORM never interposes a mock between Python and PostgreSQL, any test that calls a terminal method exercises the live database including its integrity constraints. Which means missing or mis-scoped constraints are testable: a NOT NULL that should exist and doesn't, a UNIQUE index that's too broad or too narrow, an absent foreign key. You attempt the operation and assert that psycopg3 raises IntegrityError. Schema correctness becomes something your test suite covers, with no infrastructure beyond pytest.

Meanwhile the predicate-structure tests from part 4 need only a schema-consistent database, not populated data. half_orm dev patch apply also generates a read-only base test per relation that checks it's instantiable, that it subclasses Relation, and that every declared Fkeys alias points at a real PostgreSQL constraint and returns a Relation. Break an alias with a patch and the suite tells you at merge time.

docs.title: What this costs
docs.text:
Workflow compliance is required. This is the one genuinely soft guarantee in the whole design. The runtime dissolutions from earlier posts are model-level: you can't write an N+1 because the mechanism doesn't exist. This one is procedural: it holds as long as every schema change goes through a patch. A DBA who runs ALTER TABLE directly against production breaks the version invariant, and the divergence has to be reconciled before the next patch applies. If your organisation can't commit to that, you get much less out of this than the design promises.

History is strictly linear. Long-lived feature branches that evolve the schema differently from ho-prod are not supported. That's the price of the co-deployment guarantee: a linear, fully audited schema history is what makes "pull, upgrade, restart" safe.

No automatic down-migrations. Rollback returns you to a release that shipped, not through an inverse of the change you are undoing. For a lot of schema changes that's the honest answer anyway (an automatically generated down-migration for a destructive DDL statement is frequently a comforting fiction), but if your process depends on reversible migrations, this is a real difference.

docs.title: The through-line
docs.text:
Six essays, one idea: give the schema exclusive authority, and the problems that come from splitting authority stop existing.

At runtime, that means no identity map, no session, no lazy loading, no N+1, no proprietary query language: not because those were solved, but because the concepts they need have no counterpart in a schema-first relational model. Over time, it means schema and code in one commit, patches in plain SQL, git as the authoritative history, and a checkout that carries the database rather than instructions for rebuilding it.

Ted Neward's essay ended by observing that the traditional answers to the impedance mismatch amount to "effectively 'solving' the problem by ignoring one half of it." He meant that as a criticism.

halfORM covers exactly half of SQL: the data-manipulation half. It has nothing to say about CREATE TABLE, and that's the point: DDL belongs to the database and the people who administer it. I'd argue that's the right half to cover, and that covering it well is enough.

half-orm-dev lives in its own repository: half-orm/half-orm-dev.

docs.title: You Can't Have an N+1 Problem if Navigation Isn't a Query
docs.text:
Part 3 of six in Relation-Oriented Programming. Series index

The examples use the four-table blog schema of the running example: author, post, comment, comment_type.

Every Python developer who has shipped a Django app has written this bug:

# One query for the posts, then one more per post for the author
for post in Post.objects.filter(published=True):
    print(post.author.name)      # N implicit queries

A hundred posts, a hundred and one queries. The fix is well known:

for post in Post.objects.filter(published=True).select_related('author'):
    print(post.author.name)      # one query now

Notice what kind of fix that is. It's an opt-in, at every call site, forever. Nothing in the first version is wrong-looking. It reads exactly like the code you meant to write. The framework chose, on your behalf, to make attribute access capable of hitting the database, and then handed you a flag to undo that choice one query at a time. Miss the flag and you get a performance bug that looks like correct code and only shows up under load.

Part 2 established that a halfORM Relation is a predicate over a set of rows and that nothing touches the database until a terminal method runs. Apply that to foreign keys and the N+1 problem stops being a thing you can write.

# One query, with a JOIN. No opt-in, no configuration, no flag to forget.
for row in Post(published=True).fk_author():
    print(row['name'])

fk_author() does not fetch an author. It returns a new Relation on blog.author, restricted to the rows reachable from the current predicate through that foreign key. It adds a join constraint. No SQL is sent. The query runs once, when iteration begins.

There's no fetch strategy to configure, because there's no fetching to strategise about. The problem isn't tuned down; it's unreachable.

docs.title: Every foreign key is navigable, with no configuration
docs.text:
At startup halfORM introspects the live PostgreSQL catalog: tables, views, columns, primary keys, foreign-key constraints, inheritance links. That costs a one-time hit at connection: roughly 19 ms for a four-table schema, 26 ms for pagila's 23 relations, 384 ms for a GitLab-sized schema of 880 relations.

Out of that metadata, every FK constraint is bound as an instance attribute under its constraint name, in both directions. If post declares a foreign key to author, you get the forward key on Post and a reverse key on Author, named by convention _reverse_fkey_<database>_<schema>_<table>_<field>. That first component is the database name, which is why blog appears twice below: the database and the schema happen to share a name here. Nothing is declared in Python. Nothing is configured. Print a bare relation and it tells you what's available:

>>> print(Author())
# DATABASE: blog | SCHEMA: blog | TABLE: author
# FIELDS:
# - id:    (uuid) NOT NULL
# - name:  (text) NOT NULL
# - email: (text) NOT NULL
# PRIMARY KEY (id)
# FOREIGN KEYS:
# - _reverse_fkey_blog_blog_comment_author_id: ("id")
# - _reverse_fkey_blog_blog_post_author_id: ("id")
#
# Fkeys = {
#     'rfk_blog_blog_comment_author_id': '_reverse_fkey_blog_blog_comment_author_id',
#     'rfk_blog_blog_post_author_id': '_reverse_fkey_blog_blog_post_author_id',
# }

That last block is a ready-to-paste template. Copy it into the class body, rename the keys to something you'd actually want to type, drop the ones you don't need:

class Author(...):
    Fkeys = {
        'rfk_posts': '_reverse_fkey_blog_blog_post_author_id',
    }

class Post(...):
    Fkeys = {
        'fk_author':    'post_author_id_fkey',
        'rfk_comments': '_reverse_fkey_blog_blog_comment_post_id',
    }

The convention is fk_ for a direct, many-to-one key and rfk_ for a reverse, one-to-many key, but it's only a convention; pick your own names. And aliases are strictly optional ergonomics. author.rfk_blog_blog_post_author_id() works from the moment you instantiate the model; author.rfk_posts() is the same thing with a name you enjoy reading.

This is the part that's hard to appreciate until you've used it. There is no model file. There is no Table(...) per relation, no models.ForeignKey(...), no mapping configuration, no relationship() with a back_populates. The schema already says all of that. It said it in DDL, which is the language for saying it.

docs.title: Chained navigation is still one query
docs.text:
author = Author(name='Alice')

# Authors who have commented on Alice's posts: one query, three joins
author.rfk_posts().rfk_comments().fk_author()

Each step extends the relational expression. Nothing executes. The join conditions come from the FK constraints recorded in the catalog, so there is nothing to state and nothing to get wrong.

Combine that with the set operators from part 2 and the expressions start reading like the question you were asked:

# Authors who have commented but never written a post
Comment().fk_author() - Post().fk_author()

# Authors who have both posted and commented
Post().fk_author() & Comment().fk_author()

# Authors who commented on published posts
Post(published=True).rfk_comments().fk_author()

No Python loop anywhere. Each of those is one SQL query.

FK aliases also take keyword arguments, so a join and an additional filter on the target are a single expression:

post.fk_author(name=('ilike', 'a%'))

And crucially, unlike ORM eager loading (which applies a loading strategy across all mapped associations), only the associations you actually navigate are joined. Nothing else. The join graph is exactly what you wrote.

docs.title: Navigating vs. joining in place
docs.text:
Each FK attribute supports two modes, and the difference matters once you want nested results.

Calling it (post.fk_author()) navigates: you get a Relation on the target table and you've moved.

Calling .set() on it (alice.rfk_posts.set()) activates the join without moving: alice is still an Author predicate, but the join to post is now live. Which lets ho_select aggregate the joined rows:

alice = Author(name='Alice')
alice.rfk_posts.set()

for row in alice.ho_select(json_agg={'rfk_posts': ['id', 'title']}):
    print(row['name'], row['rfk_posts'])
    # row['rfk_posts'] == [{'id': ..., 'title': '...'}, ...]

One query. PostgreSQL's json_agg does the nesting server-side. The return type follows the FK direction: a reverse key (one-to-many) gives you a list of dicts, a direct key (many-to-one) gives you a single dict or None.

This covers the nested-retrieval case that would otherwise push you to a view or to raw SQL: the "give me each author with their posts" shape that classical ORMs answer with prefetch_related and two queries stitched together in Python.

docs.title: The honest part: joins make duplicates
docs.text:
SQL operates on multisets. The relational model doesn't. Compose two navigated expressions with a set operator and the generated SQL can hand you the same row more than once. Take the published posts written by Alice or by Bob:

published  = Post(published=True)
all_theirs = (Author(name='Alice').rfk_posts() |
              Author(name='Bob').rfk_posts())

result = list((published & all_theirs).ho_select())
# Warning: 3 duplicate(s) removed in ho_select on Post.
#          Consider using distinct=True for better performance.

Both operands of the | reach post by navigating from author, so the intersection carries two paths to the same table, and a post can arrive by both. halfORM removes duplicates by primary key, so correctness is preserved regardless, and warns you. Passing distinct=True silences the warning and delegates deduplication to PostgreSQL, which is what you want on a large result set:

list((published & all_theirs).ho_select(distinct=True))

Often there's a formulation that avoids the issue entirely by starting from the other end. The same question, asked from author instead of from post:

list(Author(name=('in', ['Alice', 'Bob'])).rfk_posts(published=True))

That is one hop from author to post, so no row can arrive twice. The two expressions denote the same set and generate structurally different SQL; which one you write depends on which relation is the natural starting point for the question.

Two limitations. DISTINCT isn't applied automatically everywhere, because duplicates are sometimes intentional (ho_count() especially), so the opt-in stays explicit. And tables without a primary key, plus views (which have no PK by definition), can't benefit from PK-based deduplication at all. For those, rows come back as-is and it's on you to pass distinct=True, or on the view definition to produce a set in the first place.

docs.title: You can always see the SQL
docs.text:
Since there's no cache and no query rewriting layer, what you wrote is what runs, and you can check:

published = Post(published=True)
q = (published.fk_author(name=('ilike', 'alice%')) |
     published.fk_author(name=('ilike', 'john%')))
q.ho_mogrify()
list(q)
# select
#   r1.*
# from
#   "blog"."author" as r1
#   join "blog"."post" as r2 on
#     (r2."author_id" = r1."id")  and
#     (r2."published" = true::bool)
# where
#   ((r1."name" ilike 'alice%'::text) or
#   (r1."name" ilike 'john%'::text))

Two navigations combined with | produce one join, with published folded into the ON clause and the two name predicates merged into a single WHERE. Setting model.sql_trace = True logs every query along with the Python file and line that caused it.

There's also a predicate-level view, before any query exists. repr() on a navigated relation shows the whole join structure, with each target's own constraints nested inside:

q = published.fk_author(name=('ilike', 'alice%'))
repr(q)
# DATABASE: blog  |  SCHEMA: blog  |  TABLE: author
# FIELDS:
# - id:    (uuid) NOT NULL
# - name:  (text) NOT NULL    (name ilike alice%)
# - email: (text) NOT NULL
# FOREIGN KEYS:
# - _reverse_fkey_blog_blog_post_author_id: ("id")
#      TABLE: post
#      FIELDS:
#      - id:        (uuid) NOT NULL
#      - title:     (text) NOT NULL
#      - published: (bool) NOT NULL  (published = True)
#      - author_id: (uuid)

You can read the query you're about to run without running it.

Since every predicate compiles to plain parameterised SQL over psycopg3, there's no runtime overhead relative to hand-written queries. Performance is PostgreSQL and the network. The only framework cost is that one-time introspection at startup.

docs.title: The general shape
docs.text:
An N+1 problem requires that traversing a relationship be capable of issuing a query. Remove that capability and the bug class goes with it: not as a default you could change, not as a lint rule, not as a flag you have to remember. There is no code you can write that produces it.

That's what "structurally precluded" means, and it's the same move as the last post's: don't solve the problem, remove the concept it needs in order to exist.

Next: what this does to the shape of a codebase, specifically why the Repository pattern stops earning its keep.

Foreign-key navigation is documented in FKey, and worked through end to end in Simple Blog.

docs.title: Delete Your Repository Layer
docs.text:
Part 4 of six in Relation-Oriented Programming. Series index

Here's a question about a blog schema of four tables: author, post, comment, and comment_type, whose DDL is in the series index. Who are the reviewers of a given post? A reviewer is an author who left a comment of type review on it.

In any ORM codebase written in the last fifteen years, the answer lives in a service or a repository, and it looks like this:

class PostService:
    def get_reviewers(self, post_id):
        return (session.query(Author)
            .join(Comment, Comment.author_id == Author.id)
            .join(CommentType, Comment.comment_type == CommentType.name)
            .filter(Comment.post_id == post_id,
                    CommentType.name == 'review').all())

One method, three tables, every join condition spelled out, and one class that has to know the internal structure of all three relations at once.

Now the same question in halfORM:

class CommentType(db.get_relation_class('blog.comment_type')):
    Fkeys = {'rfk_comments': ...}

    def reviews(self):
        return CommentType(name='review').rfk_comments()

class Comment(db.get_relation_class('blog.comment')):
    Fkeys = {'fk_comment_type': ..., 'fk_author': ...}

    def reviewers(self):
        return self.fk_comment_type().reviews().fk_author()

class Post(db.get_relation_class('blog.post')):
    Fkeys = {'rfk_comments': ...}

    def reviewers(self):
        return self.rfk_comments().reviewers()

Three one-line methods, each on the class of the relation it describes, each delegating to its neighbour. No join condition appears anywhere. The query assembles itself as the delegation chain unwinds, and Post(id=42).reviewers() produces a single SQL query with three joins.

I call this predicate locality: every business predicate belongs on the Relation subclass of the entity it describes. It is, as far as I can tell, the most consequential thing about relation-oriented programming that isn't about queries at all.

docs.title: Three properties fall out
docs.text:
It's set-general. Post.reviewers() works on any Post predicate. One post, all published posts, every post by a given author, with no modification:

Post(id=42).reviewers()                       # reviewers of one post
Post(published=True).reviewers()              # reviewers of all published posts
Author(name='Alice').rfk_posts().reviewers()  # reviewers of Alice's posts

The service version takes a post_id. To ask the second question you either call it in a loop (and now you have an N+1 problem in your service layer) or you rewrite it to accept a collection and rewrite the filter to match. The halfORM version never knew how many posts there were, because the argument was never a post id. It was a set.

Knowledge stays where it belongs. Post.reviewers() has no idea what a review is. It knows it has comments, and it knows comments know about reviewers. The definition of "review" (the string 'review', the fact that it's a row in comment_type at all) lives in CommentType, which is the only class that should know. Rename the type, add a second reviewing type, change the semantics: you touch CommentType.reviews() and nothing else.

That's Parnas's information-hiding criterion, applied with an unusually clean decomposition rule. Parnas's hard question is always what should each module hide? Here the answer is given to you: each class hides its own slice of the schema. And the delegation chain is the Law of Demeter applied to relational navigation: no class knows anything beyond its immediate neighbours in the FK graph. Cognitive load at each node is bounded by that node's degree.

Every level is independently testable. Because each method is anchored to one relation, you can test it against that relation alone:

from half_orm.testing import (assertConstraintsMatch,
                              assertTablePath, assertSamePredicate)

REVIEW_CONSTRAINT = dict(table='blog.comment_type', field='name', value='review')

class TestCommentType(TestCase):
    def test_reviews(self):
        reviews = CommentType().reviews()
        self.assertIsInstance(reviews, Comment)
        assertConstraintsMatch(reviews, **REVIEW_CONSTRAINT)

class TestComment(TestCase):
    def test_reviewers(self):
        reviewers = Comment().reviewers()
        self.assertIsInstance(reviewers, Author)
        assertConstraintsMatch(reviewers, **REVIEW_CONSTRAINT)
        assertTablePath(reviewers,
            'blog.comment', 'blog.comment_type', 'blog.comment', 'blog.author')

    def test_reviewers_delegates_to_comment_type(self):
        comment = Comment()
        assertSamePredicate(
            comment.reviewers(),
            comment.fk_comment_type().reviews().fk_author())

class TestPost(TestCase):
    def test_reviewers(self):
        reviewers = Post(id=42).reviewers()
        self.assertIsInstance(reviewers, Author)
        assertConstraintsMatch(reviewers, table='blog.post', field='id', value=42)
        assertConstraintsMatch(reviewers, **REVIEW_CONSTRAINT)

No SQL is executed. No fixture data is required. These assertions operate on the structure of the predicate: which tables it involves, which constraints it carries, whether one method really delegates to another.

And look at REVIEW_CONSTRAINT. The same constant is asserted at all three levels. That's not repetition; it's the evidence. Post.reviewers() is correct only because the comment_type.name = 'review' constraint introduced three delegations down survives the whole chain intact. Seeing the identical constant pass at every level is a direct, readable proof that it does.

The test suite ends up isomorphic to the code, which is isomorphic to the schema. One class per relation, one test class per relation, each testing only what its class knows.

docs.title: Why the Repository pattern exists at all
docs.text:
Now the uncomfortable bit. Putting query logic on the entity class isn't just unusual in ORM codebases; it's actively discouraged. Fowler's Repository pattern and most Domain-Driven Design practice say the opposite: domain objects model behaviour, repositories own queries, and the boundary between them is load-bearing architecture.

I think that boundary is, in substantial part, a workaround.

Consider what an ORM entity actually is. It's a proxy tied to a session, carrying implicit state, with attributes that may or may not be loaded and that may issue queries when touched. Putting query logic on an object like that is dangerous: your method's behaviour depends on whether self is attached, detached, or expired; on whether the session is open; on what's already in the identity map. So the community developed the correct response to that constraint: move the queries somewhere the constraint doesn't apply. That's the Repository.

Remove the constraint and the workaround loses its reason to exist.

A halfORM Relation subclass is a stateless predicate. There's no session attachment, no identity, no lazy attribute, no loaded-or-not ambiguity. Calling a method on it composes a new predicate and returns it. There is no state to be wrong about, so there is nothing a query method on the class can break.

And the relational model imposes the decomposition criterion, rather than an architectural convention layered on top of the code: one class per relation, one predicate per business concept, anchored to the relation that holds it. The schema is the decomposition. You don't choose a module boundary and defend it in review; the foreign-key graph already drew it.

Which is not nothing, incidentally. "Where should this go?" is one of the most expensive recurring questions in a codebase, and most architectural patterns are attempts to answer it in advance. Here the answer is mechanical: which relation does this predicate constrain? That class.

docs.title: It generalises
docs.text:
The blog example is the minimal non-trivial case. The pattern holds for any acyclic FK graph. For a path R₁ →ᶠ¹ R₂ →ᶠ² ⋯ →ᶠⁿ Rₙ, a predicate defined on R₁ composes predicates on R₂ … Rₙ through n−1 delegating methods, each O(1) in code written. Depth doesn't hurt you: a five-hop query is five one-line methods, and each one is readable in isolation because none of them can see past its neighbours.

Compare that to the service-layer version at five hops, which is a single method containing five join conditions and knowledge of five tables' internals, and which has to be rewritten every time any of those five schemas changes.

docs.title: The adoption problem
docs.text:
The main thing that goes wrong when experienced developers pick up halfORM is that they keep the repository.

It's a trained habit. Years of separating mapping artefacts from business objects teaches you to treat a generated class as infrastructure (plumbing you shouldn't put domain logic into), and so people generate their model, then build a service layer on top of it and write the same joins they always wrote. It works. It just throws away most of the benefit, because now the query logic is centralised again, it isn't set-general again, and no class owns its own predicates again.

FK aliases, @singleton guards, and domain operations belong inside the Relation subclass. half-orm-dev makes this explicit in the generated files themselves, with a developer zone that the code generator is guaranteed never to touch, which is the subject of a later post in this series. But the shift is mental before it's technical, and it's the prerequisite for the rest.

If you take one thing from this essay: the Repository pattern was a correct response to session-bound entity proxies. If you don't have session-bound entity proxies, check whether you still need the response.

The testing helpers used here are documented in Testing.

docs.title: A Relation Is a Predicate, Not an Object
docs.text:
Part 2 of six in Relation-Oriented Programming. Series index

The examples use the four-table blog schema of the running example: author, post, comment, comment_type.

Last time I argued that the structural problems of ORM come from a design direction, and that inverting the direction dissolves them. This one is about the object you get at the other end of that inversion, because almost everything else follows from it.

Here is the whole idea in one line:

Author(name='Alice')

This does not fetch Alice. It does not talk to the database at all. It is the set of authors whose name is Alice: a description, not a result. In relational algebra terms, T(c1=v1, c2=v2) denotes:

σc1 = v1 ∧ c2 = v2(T)

A selection. A predicate over a set of tuples. Nothing is materialised, nothing is loaded, no connection is used, and the object you hold carries filter criteria rather than row data.

Everything below is a consequence.

docs.title: Consequence 1: no identity, therefore no session
docs.text:
A classical ORM hands you a proxy for one row and then has to answer an unanswerable question: when do two proxies denote the same row? That question is where identity maps, sessions, detached-instance errors and expired-attribute surprises all come from.

halfORM never constructs a proxy for a single entity, so the question never comes up.

# No entity loaded, no identity to track: direct update by predicate
Author(id=42).ho_update(name='Jane Doe')

There is no session to open, no unit of work to flush, no object to attach or detach. An UPDATE ... WHERE id = 42 is issued and that's the end of it.

The commitment goes all the way down to equality. a == b on two Relation objects is defined as the symmetric difference is empty:

a == b ⟺ (a ∖ b) ∪ (b ∖ a) = ∅

No primary keys involved, no memory addresses involved. Two predicates are equal when they denote the same set of rows, which is a question about data, not about memory. If both operands are literally the same Python object, the check short-circuits and no query runs; otherwise it compiles to a single SQL query and tests it for emptiness.

This sounds exotic until you notice that Python already does it: {1,2,3} == {2,3,1} is True because set.__eq__ denotes extensional equality, not object identity. Relations are sets. They get set equality.

Two honest qualifications. First, what's tested is extensional equality: given the current database state, do these two predicates denote the same rows? That is not logical equivalence (do they denote the same rows for every possible state?), which would need a query-equivalence prover. Two predicates can agree today and disagree tomorrow. Second, defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes Relation instances unhashable in Python 3, so they can't be dict keys or set members. That's deliberate: hashing a database-backed object by value would have to issue a query, and hashing is supposed to be pure and cheap. The cost is real; I'll come back to it under trade-offs.

docs.title: Consequence 2: dictionaries, not hydrated instances
docs.text:
ho_select() returns a generator of plain Python dictionaries, one per row.

for row in Author(name=('ilike', 'a%')).ho_select():
    print(row['name'], row['email'])

No hydration. No deferred columns. No lazy attributes. You can project explicitly with ho_select('id', 'name') if a wide table makes full fetches expensive, but that's a performance choice, not a correctness one: there's no object state to be partially populated, so partial loading has nothing to be partial about.

The partial-object problem doesn't get solved. It stops being expressible.

docs.title: Consequence 3: set algebra, because sets have an algebra
docs.text:
Python's operators are overloaded on Relation objects, which means composition is just arithmetic:

Python Relational algebra SQL R | S σp1(T) ∪ σp2(T) WHERE ... OR ... R & S σp1(T) ∩ σp2(T) WHERE ... AND ... R - S σp1(T) ∖ σp2(T) WHERE ... AND NOT (...) R ^ S σp1(T) △ σp2(T) symmetric difference R.fk(p) σp1(T) ⋈FK σp(U) JOIN U ON ... R.ho_select(a1, …) πa1,…(σp1(T)) SELECT a1, ...

In practice:

published   = Post(published=True)
alice_posts = Author(name='Alice').rfk_posts()
bob_posts   = Author(name='Bob').rfk_posts()

all_theirs           = alice_posts | bob_posts     # union
all_theirs_published = published & all_theirs      # intersection
silent               = Author() - Post().fk_author()  # authors who never posted

Every one of those lines is a value. Not a query: a value. No SQL has been sent. silent is a Relation you can pass to a function, store in a dict of named filters, or compose further, and it will not touch the database until someone calls a terminal method on it.

These algebraic properties aren't aspirational, either. halfORM ships a test suite that verifies the Boolean algebra laws (commutativity, associativity, distributivity, De Morgan, double complement, the relative-complement identities) and the classical relational identities, notably selection push-through join, σp(R) ⋈ S = σp(R ⋈ S) when p mentions only attributes of R. All of it against a live PostgreSQL instance. The laws are theorems; the suite tests that halfORM's compilation preserves them end to end.

docs.title: Consequence 4: deferred execution, with a short list of terminals
docs.text:
Database interaction happens at a short list of method names, and they're named after the SQL verbs rather than after a persistence vocabulary:

ho_select, ho_get, ho_count, ho_insert, ho_update, ho_delete, ho_is_empty, plus ho_copy for bulk loading through COPY FROM and an ho_a* counterpart to each of them for asyncio.

No save(), no flush(), no merge(), no persist(). The ho_ prefix exists for exactly one reason: to stay out of the way of the method names you want to use for your own business logic.

ho_select() returns a generator and issues its SQL lazily, on first iteration. The others execute immediately. And because a Relation is a set, iterating it directly does what you'd expect:

if author_filter:
    candidates = Author(name=('ilike', author_filter)).rfk_posts(published=True)
else:
    candidates = Post(published=True)

for row in candidates.ho_select(order_by='title', limit=20):
    process(row)

Ordering and pagination are arguments to the terminal method (the natural execution point) rather than mutations of the predicate. The Relation itself stays a pure description.

Comparison operators come from PostgreSQL, not from a DSL. A constructor argument of the form field=(comp, value) generates WHERE field comp value directly: ('>', 100), ('ilike', 'a%'), ('in', [1, 2, 3]). There is no __gte suffix convention to learn, because there is no query language to learn apart from SQL. When you exceed what the API expresses, model.execute_query(sql, values) runs arbitrary parameterised SQL through psycopg3 and hands you back dictionaries.

docs.title: Consequence 5: singletons are a structural property
docs.text:
Sometimes you really do mean one row. halfORM lets you say so, and checks it without querying:

# email is UNIQUE NOT NULL, so this predicate denotes at most one tuple. By definition.
Author(email='alice@example.com').ho_assert_is_singleton().ho_update(email='alice@example.org')

# name is not a key: raises NotASingletonError immediately, no round-trip
Author(name='Alice').ho_assert_is_singleton()

A predicate is a singleton when it constrains all the columns of the primary key, or all the columns of a unique not-null key, to specific values. That's a fact about the predicate and the schema; it needs no database access to establish. FK navigation inherits it: if the join fixes the target's primary key, the result is a singleton too.

For a method whose contract requires a singleton regardless of call site, there's a decorator:

class Author(...):
    @singleton
    def update_email(self, email):
        return self.ho_update(email=email)

And when you want the runtime guarantee rather than the structural one, ho_get() issues the query and raises NotFoundError or MultipleRowsError. ho_assert_is_singleton() says the predicate could match at most one row; ho_get() says it does match exactly one.

docs.title: Consequence 6: transactions are explicit, because there's nothing ambient
docs.text:
No session means no ambient transaction to silently enrol things into. The psycopg3 connection runs in autocommit, so each terminal method is its own transaction. When several must succeed or fail together, you say so:

from half_orm.relation import transaction

class Author(db.get_relation_class('blog.author')):
    @transaction
    def create_with_posts(self, posts_data):
        author = self.ho_insert()
        for post_data in posts_data:
            Post(author_id=author['id'], **post_data).ho_insert()
        return author

A per-model nesting counter handles composition: level 0→1 disables autocommit and opens a transaction; level n→n+1 creates a SAVEPOINT; coming back down releases the savepoint or rolls back to it; level 1→0 commits and restores autocommit. A helper method that is itself decorated with @transaction participates in the enclosing one through a savepoint, so it can fail and roll back partially without aborting the outer operation.

The body of the method is ordinary predicate code. Transactionality is the wrapper's concern.

One more stateless consequence, this one about destruction. ho_delete() and ho_update() on an unconstrained predicate require delete_all=True / update_all=True, because there is no session tracking your intent and no confirmation dialog between you and the whole table.

docs.title: What this costs
docs.text:
I'd rather state these than have you find them.

No cache. Every terminal method issues a query. There is no first-level or second-level cache, and there can't be one: a Relation is a predicate, not a snapshot, and its extension is evaluated against the current database state each time. Caching is an application concern.

PostgreSQL only. The whole design rests on introspecting a live catalog with a specific feature set: views, native table inheritance, advanced types. A multi-DBMS abstraction would force exactly the lowest-common-denominator trades that conventional ORMs make. If you need database portability, this isn't your library.

__eq__ is not free. The set-equality semantics is coherent inside the model and dangerous outside it. x in [r1, r2, r3] calls list.__contains__, which calls r1.__eq__(x), r2.__eq__(x), each potentially a SQL round trip, with nothing at the call site to warn you. For membership tests you control, use ho_list(*relations), which folds its operands under | into one union predicate so that x in ho_list(r1, r2, r3) dispatches to Relation.__contains__ and runs a single query. The residual risk (handing Relation objects to an external framework that calls __eq__ internally for caching or deduplication) is irreducible. Don't put them in generic containers.

Type safety. ho_select() is typed Iterator[dict[str, Any]], so your IDE can't complete column names and mypy can't catch row['naem']. That's a real cost of returning dictionaries, and it has an answer: generated TypedDicts and base classes derived from the live schema, with no schema declaration written by hand. half-orm-dev generates both from the same introspection, alongside the model itself.

Set semantics vs SQL multisets. SQL works on multisets; joins can produce duplicates that the relational model wouldn't. ho_select removes duplicate primary keys automatically and warns you to pass distinct=True so the database does it instead. More on this next time, where the joins come in.

docs.title: The shape of the thing
docs.text:
Step back and the pattern is uniform: each design decision refuses to introduce into the model any state or abstraction that has no counterpart in the relational model itself. No identity, because sets don't have identity. No hydrated state, because tuples aren't objects. No ambient transaction, because there's no session to host one. No proprietary query language, because SQL already exists.

What's left is small, and it composes. Part 3 is about the operation that makes it worth using: what happens when you follow a foreign key.

The predicate model is specified in Fundamentals and the full API in Relation.

docs.title: The Vietnam of Computer Science, Twenty Years On
docs.text:
Part 1 of six in Relation-Oriented Programming. Series index

In June 2006, Ted Neward published an essay called The Vietnam of Computer Science. Object-relational mapping, he argued, is a quagmire: easy early victories, steady mission creep, mounting costs, and no clean exit. The analogy was deliberately provocative and the essay became one of those things many developers have heard of and fewer have read.

Twenty years later, the frameworks are all still here. Hibernate, SQLAlchemy, Django ORM, ActiveRecord: none of them went away, and every one of them got bigger. Each ships its own query language on top of SQL. Each requires you to hold two models in your head at once: the object graph you wrote and the tables underneath it. That's usually where the retrospective ends: ORM is still a mess, ha ha, anyway back to work.

I want to make a sharper claim. The problems Neward catalogued are not a maturity issue that twenty more years of engineering will fix. They are consequences of a design decision that every mainstream ORM makes on its first page, and they persist because that decision persists.

docs.title: The catalogue
docs.text:
Start with the problems themselves. The literature has converged on a stable list (Ireland et al. gave the most systematic academic treatment in 2009) and six of them show up at runtime, independently of how your schema changes over time.

Identity. Your language says two things are the same when they're at the same memory address. Your database says two rows are the same when their primary keys match. An ORM has to decide when two in-memory objects denote the same tuple, and there is no clean answer once objects can be partially loaded, cached, or detached from a session. Hence identity maps. Hence DetachedInstanceError. Hence every hour you have ever spent reasoning about what a session does.

Partial object. A tuple has a fixed set of columns. An object is expected to carry complete state. So the ORM must choose: load everything eagerly, which is wasteful, or defer column loads lazily, which is complex and surprising. Neither is universally right, so every framework exposes knobs and every codebase gets them wrong somewhere.

Inheritance. Class hierarchies have no relational equivalent. Table-per-hierarchy, table-per-class, table-per-concrete-class: three strategies, each trading away query complexity, normalisation, or type safety. You pick one early, you live with it for years.

Navigation, a.k.a. N+1. Walking an association either issues one query per object (the N+1 problem) or joins everything upfront whether you needed it or not. Both extremes are wrong in general, so frameworks expose per-association fetch strategies, and N+1 keeps showing up in production anyway because the fix is opt-in at every call site.

Encapsulation. The framework has to reflectively read and write every persistent field, which means your domain classes have to expose every persistent field. Your object design is now partly dictated by your persistence layer.

Query language. SQL is the native language of the relational model, but an object-centric ORM can't hand it to you directly without breaking its own abstraction. So you get HQL, JPQL, the Django ORM API, LINQ, each a partial reimplementation of a language that already existed and was already complete. You learn a dialect with its own documentation, its own edge cases, and its own version history, and at the end of it you cannot express anything you couldn't have expressed in SQL.

Then there's a seventh problem that lives on a different axis entirely.

Ownership. Who is allowed to change the schema, and how does the change reach the other side? In code-first ORMs the application claims authority: you edit a class, a migration tool generates DDL, the database follows. That works beautifully on a greenfield project and starts leaking the moment reality intrudes: a second application sharing the schema, a DBA adding an index, a schema that predates your code by a decade. Database-first tools invert the authority but usually provide no mechanism to propagate a change back into application code: rename a column and every query referencing it breaks, some of them loudly, some of them silently.

And the real difficulty underneath ownership is atomicity. A migration that renames a column must ship simultaneously with the code that uses the new name. That is structurally hard when a code generator owns the generated files, because regeneration overwrites whatever you wrote by hand.

docs.title: They aren't seven problems
docs.text:
These are not seven independent defects that happen to cluster in the same kind of software.

Identity is underneath partial objects and encapsulation both: you only need to track which object is which because objects hold state, and you only need reflective field access because the framework has to put state into them and get it back out. Lazy loading compounds navigation: N+1 exists because association traversal is allowed to issue a query behind your back, and it's allowed to do that because the framework is pretending an object graph is in memory when it isn't. Query languages exist because exposing SQL would reveal that the object facade is a facade. And ownership compounds all of it: a code-first migration tool can't regenerate your model without risking your hand-written code.

Pull on any thread and you arrive at the same knot. Every mainstream ORM starts from the commitment that the relational model should be hidden from the application developer, and that schema authority flows from application code to the database. Every one of the problems above is that commitment coming due.

This is why twenty years of engineering effort hasn't dissolved them. The effort was spent making the facade better. The facade is the problem.

docs.title: Direction, not quality
docs.text:
So the claim I want to make is narrow and, I think, falsifiable: the structural ORM problems are a consequence of design direction, not of implementation quality. Hibernate is not badly built. SQLAlchemy is a genuinely great piece of software. They are excellent implementations of a direction that generates these problems by construction.

Directions can be inverted.

Suppose you take the opposite commitment: the live database schema is the sole source of truth for the structure of your data access layer. Not "database-first" in the weak sense of designing the schema before the code, but in the strong sense that no table, no column, no type, no key, no constraint is ever declared in the host language, and the access layer reads all of it from the live catalog at startup.

What happens to the seven problems?

Identity has no meaning, because there is no entity proxy to identify: you get an object that denotes a set of rows, and a set has no identity to track. Partial objects have no meaning, because query results are plain dictionaries and nothing holds state between calls. Code-first inheritance has no meaning, because mapping only ever runs schema-to-code. N+1 has no meaning, because foreign-key navigation builds a join instead of issuing a query. Encapsulation is unconstrained, because there are no persistent fields inside the object to reflect on. And SQL remains the query language, because there is no facade left to protect.

Note the shape of those sentences. Not "solved". Not "mitigated with a well-chosen default". Has no meaning. The problems don't get fixed; the concepts they presuppose stop existing.

That's not a resolution of the impedance mismatch. It's a dissolution.

docs.title: What this series is
docs.text:
halfORM, a Python library for PostgreSQL, is built on this principle. This series takes the argument apart into pieces you can evaluate one at a time:

  1. A relation is a predicate, not an object: the core abstraction, set algebra on Python objects, and what happens to __eq__ when equality means set equality.
  2. You can't have an N+1 problem if navigation isn't a query: foreign-key navigation as join construction, with zero configuration.
  3. Delete your repository layer: why query logic can live on the relation class once there's no session, and what that does to code organisation.
  4. halfORM vs SQLAlchemy Core vs Django ORM: three queries, side by side, including the one where halfORM loses.
  5. Git is the migration tool: the ownership problem, and what schema co-evolution looks like when git is the authority rather than a migrations table.

One more thing about the name. halfORM covers exactly half of SQL: the data manipulation half (INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE). It has no opinion whatsoever about CREATE TABLE. Schema definition belongs to the database and to the people who administer it, expressed in the language designed for it.

I picked that name years before I read Neward's essay carefully enough to notice what he says near the end: the traditional answers to the impedance mismatch amount to "effectively 'solving' the problem by ignoring one half of it." He meant it as a criticism. I'd argue it's the right move, as long as you're deliberate about which half you're ignoring and who owns it instead.

The design decisions this diagnosis leads to are catalogued in Fundamentals.

docs.title: Simple Blog
docs.text: A complete, runnable example: a small blog with authors, posts and typed comments (comments / reviews / questions). The schema and the data below are not invented for this page — they are the exact fixtures used by the blog_demo end-to-end demo in half-orm-gen, where the same tables are turned into a REST API and an admin UI with a single command. Here we use them to walk through halfORM itself.

docs.title: What This Example Demonstrates
docs.text:
• A small but realistic multi-schema design (actor for identity, blog for content)
  • A lookup table (comment_type) instead of a CHECK constraint or enum
  • FK navigation in both directions (post → author, author → posts)
  • Predicate algebra to answer "posts with at least one review" style questions
  • json_agg to fetch a post with its comments in one query
  • A transactional custom method (publish) that inserts a post and its opening comment atomically

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
CREATE SCHEMA actor;
CREATE SCHEMA blog;

CREATE TABLE actor."user" (
    id    uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    name  text NOT NULL,
    email text NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE blog.comment_type (
    name text NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY
);

CREATE TABLE blog.post (
    id        uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    title     text NOT NULL,
    content   text,
    published boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
    author_id uuid REFERENCES actor."user"(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

CREATE TABLE blog.comment (
    id           uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    content      text NOT NULL,
    post_id      uuid REFERENCES blog.post(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    author_id    uuid REFERENCES actor."user"(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    comment_type text REFERENCES blog.comment_type(name)
);

Why a lookup table for comment_type?

comment, review and question could have been a CHECK constraint or a Python Enum. A table means new types can be added with an INSERT, no migration required — and it gives the column a real foreign key that halfORM can navigate, like any other relationship.

docs.title: Naming the foreign keys
docs.text:
print() gives the real, introspected FK names — verbose, but exact. Subclass each relation, register it, and give the FKs short aliases:

from half_orm.model import register

@register
class User(blog.get_relation_class('actor.user')):
    Fkeys = {
        'comment_rfk': '_reverse_fkey_blog_demo_blog_comment_author_id',
        'post_rfk':    '_reverse_fkey_blog_demo_blog_post_author_id',
    }

@register
class Post(blog.get_relation_class('blog.post')):
    Fkeys = {
        'comment_rfk': '_reverse_fkey_blog_demo_blog_comment_post_id',
        'author_fk':   'post_author_id_fkey',
    }

@register
class Comment(blog.get_relation_class('blog.comment')):
    Fkeys = {
        'post_fk':         'comment_post_id_fkey',
        'author_fk':       'comment_author_id_fkey',
        'comment_type_fk': 'comment_comment_type_fkey',
    }

@register
class CommentType(blog.get_relation_class('blog.comment_type')):
    Fkeys = {
        'comment_rfk': '_reverse_fkey_blog_demo_blog_comment_comment_type',
    }

_reverse_fkey_blog_demo_... names are qualified with the database name (blog_demo) because halfORM derives them from PostgreSQL's own catalog, which has no notion of your Python aliases — see Foreign keys for the naming rule.
